texts: mixed: the rule fires and the forming of mire-essence is covered, but "the cauldron" — first mentioned only in the main clause — is invented fresh for every boiling and is never recorded as an actual cauldron, so nothing can be asked about it and it is a different cauldron each time. Introduce it in the when-clause so the main clause can point back at it: "When a Keeper boils silken threads in sea-water in a cauldron, mire-essence forms in that cauldron."
good. the whenever rule fires with the Keeper, the silken threads, the sea-water and the mire-essence all covered, and here the cauldron is recorded as one actual cauldron the rule refers to.

mixed: the taking and the source pools are recorded correctly, but "the Keepers" is stored as a bare proper name with no link to the Keeper kind your other sentences quantify over, so this fact never reaches them (and the pool name is typed as a single tide pool). Phrase it of each Keeper, and leave "sea-water" bare so it is the same sea-water your rules name: "Each Keeper takes sea-water from the Salt-bloom Tide-pools."

mixed: the denial is recorded, but only as a flat kind-to-kind statement that never reaches any particular water, so the reasoner cannot use it to rule out a specific batch — unlike "Ordinary oil does not produce mist-light", which did become a rule reaching each oil. The difference is that "fresh water" is read as one fused kind; break the adjective out to get the usable form: "Water that is fresh does not yield mire-essence."
